Title: Binary Words Containing Few Abelian Squares
Text:
BINARY WORDS CONTAINING FEW ABELIAN SQUARES
SZIL´ARD ZSOLT FAZEKAS, ADAM MAMMOLITI, ROBERT MERCAS¸, AND JAMIE SIMPSON
Abstract. In [2] Fici and Saarela conjectured that a binary word of length n contains at least ⌊n/4⌋
abelian squares. We slightly extend this conjecture and show that it holds in some special cases. In all
other cases we have the following: given a Parikh vector over a two letter alphabet we produce a word
with that Parikh vector which we conjecture contains the least possible number of abelian squares.
Keywords: abelian square, word.
1. Introduction
We use the usual notation for combinatorics of words. A word is the concatenation of letters taken
from an alphabet. In this paper we use the alphabet {a, b}, hence our words are binary. A word
containing n letters is w = w[1 . . . n], with w[i] being the ith letter and w[i . . . j] being the factor
beginning at position i and ending at position j. If i = 1 then the factor is a prefix and if j = n then
the factor is a suffix.
The length of w, written |w|, is the number of letters that w contains and |w|a and |w|b are,
respectively, the numbers of a’s and the number of b’s in w (this notation has the obvious extension
to larger alphabets). The vector [|w|a, |w|b] is the Parikh vector of w, written P(w). If w = uv where
u and v are words then vu is a conjugate of w. The complement of w is the word formed from w by
replacing each a with b and vice versa. The reverse of w is the word formed by writing w backwards.
Thus the complement and the reverse of abaab are babba and baaba respectively.
A factor w[i + 1..i + 2p] in which w[i + 1..i + p] = w[i + p + 1..i + 2p] is a square.
If instead
P(w[i + 1..i + p]) = P(w[i + p + 1..i + 2p]) then w[i + 1..i + 2p] is an abelian square. In older literature,
for instance [2], it was a weak square [3]. Thus the word abaababa contains the squares aa, abab,
abaaba, baba which are also abelian squares and the abelian squares baab and aababa. Clearly a word,
its complement and its reverse each contain the same number of abelian squares. If w is a binary word
then θ(w) is the number of abelian squares in w. The following conjecture is due to Fici and Saarela
[2].
Conjecture 1. Any binary word of length n contains at least ⌊n
4 ⌋abelian squares.
Following Fici and Saarela we say that an abelian square of the form a2i or b2i for some positive
integer i is trivial. They proved the following theorem.
Theorem 2. [2] If a binary word w contains only trivial abelian squares then it satisfies Conjecture
1.
However the following theorem shows this result has limited applicability.
Theorem 3. If a binary word contains three or more powers of one letter separated by powers of the
other letter then it contains a non-trivial abelian square.
Proof. Suppose the word w contains the factor ai1bj1ai2bj2ai3 where each of i1, j1, i2, j2 and i3 is a
positive integer and suppose, without loss of generality, that j1 ≤j2. If i2 is even then w contains
the non-trivial abelian square bj1ai2bj1 and if i2 is odd then w contains the non-trivial abelian square
abj1ai2bj1.
□
On the same theme we extend the Fici-Saarela conjecture to the following:
Conjecture 4. A binary word of length n contains at least ⌊n
4 ⌋abelian squares and if it contains
exactly ⌊n
4 ⌋abelian squares then all the abelian squares are trivial.
We say M(x, n) is the least number of abelian squares that can occur in a binary word w with
|w| = n and |w|a = x. This seems difficult to work out in general but we can obtain precise values for
some low values of x and make conjectures about others.

Proof. (a) Write w as A1B1A2B2 where A1 = ah and so on. There can be no abelian square beginning

6. Discussion
We have found the minimum number of abelian squares in a word of length n on alphabet {a, b}
which contains 0,1,2 or 3 occurrences of the letter a, and by complementation, n, n −1, n −2 or n −3
occurrences. We would like to settle the cases in between. We used the two a bound to establish
the three a bound. This suggests that an induction might be possible. Another approach might be
to show that as soon as a word contains one non-trivial abelian square it must contain sufficiently
many others to reach the ⌊n/4⌋bound. Coupled with Theorem 2 this would lead to a proof of the
conjecture.
There are a number of open questions related to Fici and Saarela’s Conjecture 1. See, for instance,
the surveys [4] and [1]. One variation is to count inequivalent abelian squares rather than distinct
abelian squares. Two abelian squares are equivalent if they have the same Parikh vectors. Thus abba
and abab are distinct but equivalent. Fraenkel and Simpson [3] used a straightforward approach to
show that the number of inequivalent abelian squares in a circular binary word of length 2k + 2 is at
least k, the bound being attained by (ab)k+1.
